text: On Dummett's reconstruction of the realism/anti-realism debate about a given domain, the disagreement is sharpened into a disagreement over whether:
choices: the principle of bivalence holds for that domain — whether every statement in it is determinately either true or false, independently of our capacity to recognize which
the objects that the domain talks about are concrete spatiotemporal particulars or abstract entities
the true statements of that domain all cohere with one another within a single system
the statements of that domain possess truthmakers drawn from a fundamental level of reality
explanation: Dummett recasts realism as the acceptance of bivalence together with evidence-transcendent truth, and anti-realism as its denial for undecidable statements — turning a metaphysical dispute into one about the semantics of the domain. Options 1 and 3 concern the metaphysics of objects and truthmakers, which Dummett deliberately sets aside; option 2 describes the coherence theory of truth, a separate view about the nature of truth rather than about bivalence.
